packets.key_finding: Across three experiments including a 4,207-person sample from five European countries, default nudges significantly shift risk-taking with medium-to-large effect sizes, but implementing a default (especially one the target refuses) significantly lowers how trustworthy/honest the advice is rated, an effect mediated by perceived wealth-manager honesty.
packets.methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative multi-country European survey experiment on wealth-management default framing and question wording.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives EU-representative evidence that a default which is refused or one-size-fits-all reads as less honest — the exact dark-pattern/reputational risk the brief flags — and shows question framing (e.g., 'how much to invest' vs 'how much to leave safe') independently shifts choices, directly informing both the entry-design and slider-wording decisions.
limitations: wealth-management risk-allocation decisions, not round-up savings specifically
does not measure long-run behavioral persistence, only immediate choice and perception
packets.relevance_reason: EU consumer financial-advice setting testing exactly when a default feels helpful versus manipulative, with quantified reputational costs — the most directly usable evidence for the entry-design decision.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: A nudge that shrouded the minimum-payment autopay option cut minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, because nudged users picked autopay amounts barely above the minimum and some lost autopay protection, increasing missed payments.
packets.methodology: Field experiment on live credit card accounts with 6-month follow-up on payment behavior and debt outcomes.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly supports the support team's concern: a choice-architecture change can move a headline enrollment/behavior metric without moving the thing that actually matters (debt/savings amount), and can create new harm (missed payments) for liquidity-constrained users — exactly the trade-off the round-up entry decision must weigh.
limitations: credit card debt paydown, not a savings product
does not test opt-out vs opt-in vs active-choice framing directly, only a shrouding nudge
packets.relevance_reason: A rare consumer-financial field experiment showing a default-like nudge changes nominal behavior without changing the real outcome, with heterogeneity by liquidity — the closest analogue to the brief's core worry.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and theoretical framework for downstream (post-adoption) default effects, showing they depend on time course of choice/consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and salience of trade-offs — resolving inconsistent prior findings.
packets.methodology: Conceptual synthesis and framework-building across the consumer default-effects literature; abstract-only for empirical specifics.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives the team a structured way to predict and measure which users will disengage after opt-out enrollment (weak antecedent preference, low salience) versus which will actually use the pot — directly shapes what to instrument and watch for in the round-up rollout.
limitations: general consumer choice-architecture theory, not financial-product specific
no effect sizes since it's a conceptual synthesis, not primary data
packets.relevance_reason: The literature's own general-purpose framework for exactly the persistence/disengagement question the brief asks about, in a consumer (not employer) frame.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: In 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions, 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out cost together (friction complementarity); adding a 15% tip option to the 20/25/30% menu captures 69% of achievable consumer welfare gain at only 5.4% revenue cost.
packets.methodology: Structural model estimated on 8.6 million transaction records plus an independent stated-preference survey to identify true preferences separate from default influence.
packets.why_it_matters: Provides a transferable method — a structural decomposition of why people accept a preset menu option and a counterfactual tool for choosing which value to add/preset — directly applicable to deciding which round-up multiplier (1x/2x/5x) to preset and what a welfare-minimizing menu looks like.
limitations: tipping decisions, not a financial savings product
no persistence or longitudinal outcome measured, single-decision setting
packets.relevance_reason: Explicit method transfer: a structural friction/menu-design model for preset-option adherence and welfare trade-offs, directly usable for the multiplier-level decision even though the underlying transactions are taxi tips.
packets.title: Defaults and Decisions: Choice Architecture and Consumer Opt-Out
packets.abstract:
Why do consumers accept defaults (preset or suggested options)? This paper estimates a structural model that disentangles two frictions underlying default adherence: a deviation cost (the disutility when the final choice differs from the consumer’s ideal) and an opt-out cost (the effort to override the default). I estimate the model on 8.6 million tipping decisions from NYC Yellow taxi trips. A stated-preference survey identifies consumer tipping preferences independently of defaults. The central finding is friction complementarity: 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of both frictions; remove either friction and the remaining one alone cannot sustain default adherence. Structural parameters are approximately stable when default options change, consistent with defaults channeling behavior through choice frictions rather than reshaping preferences. Counterfactual analysis shows that adding a 15% tip option below the existing 20%–25%–30% menu captures 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
 This paper was accepted by Dube, Jean-Pierre, marketing.
 Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05272 .

packets.key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts cuts unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, implying market-wide savings of £170-240 million.
packets.methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments at major UK banks.
packets.why_it_matters: Demonstrates that automatic (opt-out style) enrollment into a low-friction banking feature produces large, quantifiable consumer financial benefits in the exact UK consumer-banking setting the round-up feature will operate in.
limitations: studies alert enrollment, not a savings contribution decision
does not report the alert feature's own disengagement or opt-out rate
packets.relevance_reason: Same consumer-banking, self-directed, field-experiment setting as the product being built, showing default enrollment into a bank feature at scale changes real financial outcomes.
packets.title: Sending Out an SMS: Automatic Enrollment Experiments for Overdraft Alerts
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT At‐scale field experiments at major U.K. banks show that automatic enrollment into “just‐in‐time” text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft and unpaid item charges 17% to 19% and arranged overdraft charges 4% to 8%, implying annual market‐wide savings of £170 million to £240 million. Incremental benefits from “early‐warning” alerts are statistically insignificant, although economically significant effects are not ruled out. Prior to the experiments, over half of overdrafts could have been avoided by using lower‐cost liquidity available in savings and credit card accounts. Alerts help consumers achieve less than half of these potential savings.

packets.key_finding: Maps EU laws on dark patterns to a taxonomy of six autonomy-violation categories, showing EU regulation of pre-selected defaults and similar practices is grounded in protecting consumer autonomy.
packets.methodology: Legal/doctrinal analysis and normative taxonomy construction; abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly informs whether an opt-out enrollment design risks being classified as a dark pattern under EU law, which should shape the choice between opt-out and active-choice designs.
limitations: legal/normative analysis, not empirical
no effect sizes on enrollment or engagement
not specific to financial products
packets.relevance_reason: Gives the EU regulatory framework for judging whether a default reads as helpful or manipulative, the reputational risk the brief flags explicitly.
packets.title: Regulating Dark Patterns
packets.abstract: Dark patterns have become increasingly pervasive in online choice architectures, encompassing practices like subscription traps, hiding information about fees, pre-selecting options by default, nagging, and drip pricing. Regulators around the world have started to express concerns that such practices are causing substantial consumer detriment. This Article focuses on the legal response to dark patterns in the European Union. It provides the first comprehensive mapping of European Union laws expressly addressing dark patterns. The Article argues that these laws protect biased consumers and adopt autonomy as a normative lens to assess dark patterns. Consequently, regulating dark patterns in European Union law means regulating for autonomy. This normative lens is under-researched. This Article addresses this gap in research with two principle contributions. First, it works out a specific conception of autonomous decision-making, rooted in the paradigm that providing consumers with information enables consumers to make an informed decision. Second, the Article offers a novel normative classification for dark patterns in online choice architectures. It develops a taxonomy encompassing six categories of autonomy violations, specifically tailored for the assessment and regulation of dark patterns that exploit consumer behavioral biases. These categories serve multiple purposes. They uncover and make explicit the autonomy violations addressed by existing European Union laws. They delineate the contentious line between acceptable influences on consumer decision-making and autonomy violations that may warrant regulation in online choice architectures. They also provide policymakers in the EU and elsewhere with a framework when deliberating the regulation of other instances of dark patterns.

packets.key_finding: With a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees had not opted out after 12 months (versus ~50% non-opt-out under lower defaults elsewhere), and non-opters anchored at an income-suboptimal 12% rate.
packets.methodology: Administrative panel data from a firm with an unusually high default contribution rate; abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Shows the default level itself shapes both enrollment persistence and anchoring, evidence for how a high pre-set round-up multiplier could both raise and distort savings behavior.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k) plan, not a consumer app
single-firm case study
packets.relevance_reason: Directly tests anchoring on a high default level and 12-month opt-out persistence, close in structure to the round-up multiplier decision even though the setting is a retirement plan.
packets.title: Automatic Enrollment with a 12% Default Contribution Rate
packets.abstract: We study a retirement savings plan with a default contribution rate of 12% of income, which is much higher than previously studied defaults. Twenty-five percent of employees had not opted out of this default 12 months after hire; a literature review finds that the corresponding fraction in plans with lower defaults is approximately one-half. Because only contributions above 12% were matched by the employer, 12% was likely to be a suboptimal contribution rate for employees. Employees who remained at the 12% default contribution rate had average income that was approximately one-third lower than would be predicted from the relationship between salaries and contribution rates among employees who were not at 12%. Defaults may influence low-income employees more strongly in part because these employees face higher psychological barriers to active decision making. Contributions: conceptualized paper (JB, DL, BM, JC), wrote paper (JB, JC), edited paper (DL), implemented empirical analysis (JB, RG), project leadership (JB, JC). The research reported herein was supported by the U.S. Social Security Administration (SSA) through grant #10-M-98363-1-02 to the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) as part of the Retirement Research Consortium (RRC). The findings and conclusions expressed are solely those of the authors and do not represent the views of SSA, any agency of the Federal Government, the RRC, the authors’ universities, or NBER. The authors thank Joshua Rauh and two anonymous reviewers for their comments and thank Yeguang Chi and Richard Lombardo for excellent research assistance. The authors also acknowledge individual and collective financial support from the National Institutes of Health (grants R01-AG021650 and T32-AG-000186) and the Pershing Square Fund for Research on the Foundations of Human Behavior.

packets.key_finding: Automatic enrollment pushed 401(k) participation above 85% at three firms, but about 80% of participants initially accepted both the low default savings rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, and half still did so after three years, with offsetting effects on wealth accumulation.
packets.methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large firms' 401(k) plans.
packets.why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a pre-set default level anchors most people at that exact level for years — the direct precedent for worrying that a pre-selected round-up multiplier will anchor most users rather than let them choose their true preferred level.
limitations: employer 401(k) plan with employer-selected defaults, not a consumer app
predates the fintech/EU regulatory context the brief says has since changed
packets.relevance_reason: The classic anchoring-on-default-level study the current literature still argues with; directly informs the level/preset decision even though the setting is dated and employer-based.
packets.title: Perspectives on the Economics of Aging
packets.abstract: In the last several years, many employers have decided to automatically enroll their new employees in the company 401(k) plan.Using several years of administrative data from three large firms, we analyze the impact of automatic enrollment on 401(k) participation rates, savings behavior, and asset accumulation.We find that although employees can opt out of the 401(k) plan, few choose to do so.As a result, automatic enrollment has a dramatic impact on retirement savings behavior: 401(k) participation rates at all three firms exceed 85%, but participants tend to anchor at a low default savings rate and in a conservative default investment vehicle.We find that initially, about 80% of participants accept both the default savings rate (2% or 3% for our three companies) and the default investment fund (a stable value or money market fund).Even after three years, half of the plan participants subject to automatic enrollment continue to contribute at the default rate and invest their contributions exclusively in the default fund.The effects of automatic enrollment on asset accumulation are not straightforward.While higher participation rates promote wealth accumulation, the low default savings rate and the conservative default investment fund undercut accumulation.In our sample, these two effects are roughly offsetting on average.However, automatic enrollment does increase saving in the lower tail of the savings distribution by dramatically reducing the fraction of employees who do not participate in the 401(k) plan.

packets.key_finding: A randomized nudge (credit card payment reminders) on a Brazilian financial management platform cut late-payment fees by 14% but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% fee increase while other users saved 15%.
packets.methodology: Randomized field experiment with a consumer financial management platform in Brazil.
packets.why_it_matters: Shows a well-intentioned nudge in a consumer fintech app can help most users while making a vulnerable subgroup worse off, directly the distributional risk the brief warns against building for on average.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrollment defaults or round-up savings specifically
single-country consumer credit context, not an EU savings app
packets.relevance_reason: A closely analogous fintech field experiment showing heterogeneous, sometimes harmful, effects of a helpful-seeming nudge — exactly the distributional risk the brief asks the team to check for before defaulting everyone in.
packets.title: Side Effects of Nudging: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in the Credit Card Market
packets.abstract: Abstract This paper studies the direct and indirect effects of nudging, by means of a field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil. Reminders for upcoming credit card payments reduced credit card late-payment fees by 14%, but increased overdraft fees in checking accounts by 9%. The unintended effect is concentrated in users with a history of overdraft use. These users experienced a net increase of 5% in total fees, while the rest experienced savings of 15%. The results provide clear insights for nudge design: like any policy action, nudges can have side effects, and one size may not fit all.

packets.key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment raised participation above 85% at three firms, but about 80% of participants accepted the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and default fund, with half still at the default after three years.
packets.methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large firms comparing automatic versus standard enrollment.
packets.why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that defaults both massively raise nominal enrollment and strongly anchor the contribution level for years, directly the tension the brief poses between enrollment lift and just relocating people to a low pre-set level.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k), not a consumer app
pre-dates the mobile/EU regulatory context the brief says has changed the calculus
packets.relevance_reason: The foundational default-and-anchoring study that all subsequent enrollment-design literature, including this project's question, argues with or extends.
packets.title: For Better or For Worse: Default Effects and 401(k) Savings Behavior
packets.abstract: In the last several years, many employers have decided to automatically enroll their new employees in the company 401(k) plan. Using several years of administrative data from three large firms, we analyze the impact of automatic enrollment on 401(k) participation rates, savings behavior, and asset accumulation. We find that although employees can opt out of the 401(k) plan, few choose to do so. As a result, automatic enrollment has a dramatic impact on retirement savings behavior: 401(k) participation rates at all three firms exceed 85%, but participants tend to anchor at a low default savings rate and in a conservative default investment vehicle. We find that initially, about 80% of participants accept both the default savings rate (2% or 3% for our three companies) and the default investment fund (a stable value or money market fund). Even after three years, half of the plan participants subject to automatic enrollment continue to contribute at the default rate and invest their contributions exclusively in the default fund. The effects of automatic enrollment on asset accumulation are not straightforward. While higher participation rates promote wealth accumulation, the low default savings rate and the conservative default investment fund undercut accumulation. In our sample, these two effects are roughly offsetting on average. However, automatic enrollment does increase saving in the lower tail of the savings distribution by dramatically reducing the fraction of employees who do not participate in the 401(k) plan.

alternates.key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive even when the default option causes substantial welfare losses; active choice appears driven by random transitory attention rather than stable attentiveness.
alternates.methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default options in Medicare Part D administrative data.
alternates.why_it_matters: Strong evidence that default persistence is not conditional on the default being a good fit — relevant to whether an opt-out round-up default will keep unsuitable users enrolled regardless of harm, and that 'active choosers' may just be randomly attentive rather than genuinely engaged.
limitations: health insurance for low-income beneficiaries, not a consumer financial/savings product
no employer-vs-consumer distinction is discussed
alternates.relevance_reason: Rigorous natural-experiment evidence on default persistence and the fragility of active choice, useful by analogy though outside the financial-product domain.
alternates.title: The Behavioral Foundations of Default Effects: Theory and Evidence from Medicare Part D
alternates.abstract: We show in two natural experiments that default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization of low-income beneficiaries. The implications of this phenomenon for welfare and optimal policy depend on the sensitivity of passivity to the value of the default option. Using random assignment to default options, we show that beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive, even when enrolling in the default option would result in substantial drug consumption losses. A third natural experiment suggests that variation in active choice is driven by random transitory shocks rather than the inherent attentiveness of some beneficiaries.

alternates.key_finding: Across nine 401(k) plans, automatic enrollment raises steady-state savings rates by only 0.6% of income and default auto-escalation by only 0.3%, once job turnover, pre-vesting withdrawals, and auto-escalation opt-outs are accounted for; only 40% of defaulted employees escalate on the first scheduled date.
alternates.methodology: Longitudinal administrative data analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating employee separation, balance withdrawal, and auto-escalation opt-out dynamics.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly undercuts the 'defaults will lift enrolment, full stop' argument by showing medium/long-run leakage erodes most of the headline effect — the single best quantified rebuttal to the internal pro-default argument, even though the mechanism (vesting, job turnover) doesn't map onto a liquid consumer app.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans with employer vesting and job-turnover dynamics that don't exist in a consumer savings app
does not study opt-in or active-choice designs, only opt-out and auto-escalation
alternates.relevance_reason: The clearest quantified statement that default effects shrink substantially over time, matching the brief's explicit request for a paper contradicting the 'defaults always help' premise.
alternates.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
alternates.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

alternates.key_finding: Removing an auto-enrollment policy and adding a minor application 'ordeal' step reduced health insurance enrollment by 33%, differentially excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people.
alternates.methodology: Natural experiment studying removal of an auto-enrollment policy in a health insurance selection market.
alternates.why_it_matters: Shows that friction removed by opt-out defaults protects exactly the populations least likely to actively opt in, informing the brief's concern about who is helped versus hurt by enrollment design.
limitations: health insurance selection market, not a savings product
adverse selection dynamics specific to insurance may not apply to savings
alternates.relevance_reason: Quantifies how much friction (the opposite of a default) excludes disadvantaged users, directly informing the distributional question of who opt-in enrollment would leave out.
alternates.title: Do Ordeals Work for Selection Markets? Evidence from Health Insurance Auto-Enrollment
alternates.abstract: Are application hassles, or “ordeals,” an effective way to limit public program enrollment? We provide new evidence by studying (removal of) an auto-enrollment policy for health insurance, adding an extra step to enroll. This minor ordeal has a major impact, reducing enrollment by 33 percent and differentially excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people. Using a simple model, we show adverse selection—a classic feature of insurance markets—undermines ordeals’ standard rationale of excluding low-value individuals since they are also low-cost and may not be inefficient. Our analysis illustrates why ordeals targeting is unlikely to work well in selection markets. (JEL D82, G22, H75, I13, I18)

alternates.key_finding: Using 41 million observations, automatic (passive) employer contributions raise total saving substantially, while active-choice tax subsidies induce only about 1 cent of extra saving per $1 of subsidy, because 85% of individuals are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies.
alternates.methodology: Population-level Danish administrative panel data on savings and retirement accounts.
alternates.why_it_matters: The foundational large-scale evidence for the passive-versus-active savings distinction underlying the internal 'defaults lift enrolment' argument, though drawn from a tax-subsidy retirement context.
limitations: retirement accounts with government tax subsidies, not a consumer app
outside the 2020s app/regulatory context the brief says has changed the calculus
alternates.relevance_reason: Provides the classic large-N evidence for the passive-versus-active savings distinction underlying the active-choice design question, which current work in this space still argues with.
alternates.title: Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts: Evidence from Denmark *
alternates.abstract: Abstract Using 41 million observations on savings for the population of Denmark, we show that the effects of retirement savings policies on wealth accumulation depend on whether they change savings rates by active or passive choice. Subsidies for retirement accounts, which rely on individuals to take an action to raise savings, primarily induce individuals to shift assets from taxable accounts to retirement accounts. We estimate that each $1 of government expenditure on subsidies increases total saving by only 1 cent. In contrast, policies that raise retirement contributions if individuals take no action—such as automatic employer contributions to retirement accounts—increase wealth accumulation substantially. We estimate that approximately 15% of individuals are “active savers” who respond to tax subsidies primarily by shifting assets across accounts; 85% of individuals are “passive savers” who are unresponsive to subsidies but are instead heavily influenced by automatic contributions made on their behalf. Active savers tend to be wealthier and more financially sophisticated. We conclude that automatic contributions are more effective at increasing savings rates than subsidies for three reasons: (i) subsidies induce relatively few individuals to respond, (ii) they generate substantial crowd-out conditional on response, and (iii) they do not increase the savings of passive individuals, who are least prepared for retirement.

alternates.key_finding: Auto-enrollment's boost to participation and contributions, replicated at 12 months across 100+ US plans and a UK panel, is substantially attenuated by 36 months, with only modest average savings gains at the longer horizon though inequality in savings is reduced; a life-cycle model fits the pattern with a switching cost of about $250.
alternates.methodology: Administrative panel data from over 100 US retirement plans plus a representative UK panel; structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly answers the brief's persistence question with a specific horizon comparison (12 vs. 36 months), showing the default effect on amounts saved (not just nominal enrollment) shrinks over time even as it narrows inequality — a nuanced version of the 'vanity enrollment' concern.
limitations: retirement plan context with a $250 switching-cost estimate specific to that setting
no employer-vs-consumer mechanism discussion
alternates.relevance_reason: Gives a quantified medium-run attenuation estimate exactly matching the brief's request for whether default effects persist at 6-12+ months and whether they change amounts saved.
alternates.title: Default Options and Retirement Saving Dynamics
alternates.abstract: Using data from over 100 US retirement plans and a representative UK panel, I document the impact of auto-enrollment (AE) on retirement savings at different horizons. I replicate the impact of AE on participation and contributions in the short run (at 12 months), but I show that these gains are attenuated over the medium run (at 36 months). At this longer horizon, the average savings increases are modest, though AE significantly lowers inequality in savings. To assess AE’s lifetime impact, I estimate a life cycle consumption-savings model that can fit the observed patterns with a switching cost of approximately $250, smaller than previous estimates. (JEL D15, G51, J26, J32)
